title: How To Build Classroom Community; It's Not What You Think what-you-think/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts a mandated weekly 'kind letter' initiative from early in his career, using it as an example of a well-intentioned but weak approach to building classroom community because it manufactures niceness rather than allowing it to emerge internally. He argues that being nice is the result of a strong community, not its cause, and that community built this way lacks real student investment. Drawing on retired WNBA star Lisa Leslie's reflection that she would miss teammate camaraderie more than trophies, he identifies three conditions that generate authentic team-like bonds: an enticing goal, every member being needed to achieve it, and a genuine chance of failure. He illustrates the power of these conditions with a story of his own sixth graders celebrating a Capture the Flag win, arguing that a single thirty-minute shared experience like that builds community more effectively than countless forced 'kindness' exercises.
points: Manufactured kindness exercises (like assigned compliment letters) are a weak substitute for genuine community because they lack internal motivation.
Being nice is the byproduct of strong community, not the mechanism that creates it.
Three conditions reliably generate authentic camaraderie: an enticing goal, universal necessity of every member, and real risk of failure.
A single shared experience built on those conditions can build community faster and more durably than repeated forced-kindness rituals.
quotes: The idea being, if we focus on being nice to each other, it will encourage community-like behavior. This is a popular notion today among educators. And there is nothing wrong with it. It’s nice to be nice. But it’s a weak community builder. Being nice is the result of a strong community; it’s not the cause.

Being nice, kind, and appreciative are wonderful traits, but merely telling students to be nice or making them pretend to be nice via kind letters and community circles carries little meaning because it doesn’t come from the students themselves.
She said she would miss the camaraderie of being with her teammates. The close bonds she developed during her career meant more to her than any of the external rewards she received.
The collective action of pursuing a worthy goal builds camaraderie, teamwork, and togetherness like nothing else and will impact your students more profoundly than a thousand kind letters.
Students who in previous years would have nothing to do with each other were walking arm-and-arm and chatting excitedly.
A thirty-minute experience like this is priceless and will build community far better than coercing mumbled platitudes from students during class meetings.
